meta.regime: The market is still unwinding a war premium, but it has moved past the easy phase into the phase where the unwind starts damaging the currencies that were long it. Crude has fallen a fourth straight session on the Iran-Oman corridor framework, and the fallout is no longer confined to the loonie: the kiwi's entire inflation overshoot was petrol, and the franc's entire haven bid was the war. At the same time the American data refused to break - core PCE in line, Q2 GDP unrevised at 1.5%, claims at 206k - so the dollar's disinflation-plus-recession story has lost its second half and the hike-by-year-end probability has climbed back toward three-quarters. The one currency whose case is domestic rather than energy-driven is the euro, and it now has the widest gap on the board. The important caveat is that the de-escalation is contested: the IRGC has publicly said the Strait remains closed pending American concessions, so this is a negotiated framework with a 30-60 day talks window, not a reopening.
meta.nextBigEvent: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote, Friday Aug 28 at 14:00Z - a chair with no policy record speaking into a market that has re-priced a year-end hike to roughly 73%, on the same morning Spain's flash CPI is forecast to jump to 4.2% from 3.6% and Canadian Q2 GDP is expected at +3.4% annualised.

dailyRead: Three scores change today and they all trace back to the same force from opposite directions. The dollar is upgraded from minus 2 to minus 1 because the week's data refused to deliver the growth-and-inflation double break the market was positioned for: July core PCE printed Wednesday at +0.2% m/m and 3.3% y/y, in line rather than the feared 0.3%, headline PCE ran at 3.7% y/y, the Q2 GDP second estimate was confirmed unrevised at 1.5% annualised with personal consumption at +3.4%, its strongest since Q3 2025, and non-residential fixed investment at +8.5% on AI capex, and initial claims came in at 206k against 210k expected. September hike odds firmed to roughly 38% from 31% and a hike by year-end is now about 73% priced, with three FOMC dissents already on the record for +25bp and Collins saying on Aug 25 that it will be appropriate to tighten soon absent evidence of sustained progress. The dollar does not become strong on that - payrolls were still minus 23,000 in July and the labour market is the weak leg - but minus 2 was pricing a break that did not happen. Meanwhile the currencies that were quietly long the war premium are marked down. New Zealand is cut from plus 1 to 0: the 4.1% Q2 CPI that anchored the hawkish case was a fuel print, with transport up 10.6% and petrol up 27.5%, and the RBNZ's own July statement named the partial reopening of Hormuz as the reason it expected headline inflation to fall toward 2% over twelve months. Crude has now fallen a fourth consecutive session, WTI 80.57 and Brent 86.49, so the September 2 MPS is a genuine three-way event against a 5.6% unemployment rate that is the highest since 2015 and 2.1% wage growth; the kiwi was the worst major overnight at minus 0.34% and 0.59567. Switzerland is cut from plus 1 to 0 for the mirror-image reason: the franc's haven leg has now failed repeatedly, EUR/CHF sits near 0.938 which is no haven performance at all against the strongest currency on the board, gold slipped 0.72% to 4,624.75 as the corridor framework was announced, and what remains is a monetary profile that is purely a funding currency - July CPI 0.4% and a four-month low, core 0.3%, producer and import prices deflating, unemployment up to 3.0% - with an SNB that has explicitly signalled greater readiness to intervene against appreciation. The euro holds plus 2 and is now the widest gap on the board because its inflation problem is the only one that is domestic rather than energy-driven: July HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5%, services 3.4%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, an August composite PMI at a nine-month high of 52.1 with manufacturing at a four-year high, and a September 10 meeting where TE's model still carries a hike. The immediate euro risk is the July meeting accounts at 11:30Z today, because the gas argument has weakened - TTF is 64.36 and down 3.54%, off Monday's three-and-a-half-year high of 68.46 - and a dovish set of accounts is the main threat to plus 2; the immediate euro upside is Spain's flash August CPI tomorrow, where consensus is 4.2% against 3.6% prior, a jump large enough to move the whole area aggregate on Tuesday. Australia holds plus 1 on Tuesday's CPI beat, where the trimmed mean would not fall from 3.6% and market goods and services ex volatiles rose 1.0% in the month, with September 29 hike odds repriced to about 27% from 17%, and it now has a second independent confirmation: copper printed a fresh record at 6.6956 USD per pound against an August peak of 6.83, up 51.5% year-on-year, on LME stocks halved since mid-May, the Kamoa-Kakula flood costing up to 57,000 tonnes and more than 200,000 tonnes of tariff front-running landed at US ports in July. Japan holds plus 1 with roughly 80% priced for a 25bp move to 1.25% on September 18, July core at 1.8% and services PPI accelerating to 3.6%, though Tokyo August CPI at 23:30Z tonight carries a soft consensus of 1.7% core against 1.9% prior and is the near-term risk to that. Sterling holds plus 1 on the 6-3 hawkish split and the highest gilt yield in the G10 near 5.0%, near a six-month high at 1.36291. Canada stays at minus 1 with the tariff war live - C$27.6bn of retaliation on roughly 700 US products at 15, 25 and 50 per cent from September 8 - but note the risk honestly: Q2 GDP tomorrow at 12:30Z carries a consensus of +3.4% annualised against minus 0.1%, which is the single cleanest way for a CAD short to get hurt this week. The practical book: express the euro against the loonie, the dollar, the kiwi and now the franc; keep AUD/CAD and AUD/NZD long; take size down on every straight dollar leg ahead of Warsh Friday at 14:00Z, which is why DXY drops to a LOW-conviction short and USD/JPY steps back from HIGH to MEDIUM. And hold the geopolitical caveat in view: the IRGC said on Aug 26 that the Strait stays closed until the United States honours the Islamabad memorandum, with a senior official demanding an end to the war plus financial compensation, so a headline that re-closes this trade is available on any day.

USD.when: Sept 15-16 FOMC - hold still the base case at ~62%, but hike odds firmed to ~38% and a hike by year-end is ~73% priced
USD.note: TE re-verified this morning: policy rate 3.75% upper bound, held Jul 29 in a 9-3 vote with all three dissents FOR a hike. The upgrade to -1 is about what did NOT happen. Core PCE printed Wednesday at +0.2% m/m and 3.3% y/y, in line rather than the feared 0.3%; headline PCE ran 3.7% y/y; the Q2 GDP second estimate came in UNREVISED at 1.5% annualised, not revised lower, with personal consumption +3.4% (best since Q3 2025) and non-residential fixed investment +8.5% on AI capex; jobless claims 206k against 210k expected. Collins on Aug 25 said it will be appropriate to tighten soon absent sustained progress, and four of twelve regional Reserve Banks had already sought a discount-rate increase before the July hold. Against that, TE macro is unchanged and still soft: CPI 3.4% from 3.5%, core 2.5%, unemployment 4.1%, non-farm payrolls MINUS 23,000, average hourly earnings +0.1% m/m. Net: -1 not -2. Warsh's Jackson Hole keynote Friday at 14:00Z is a chair with no policy record speaking into a market that has re-priced a year-end hike to three-quarters - keep dollar-leg size reduced until it is delivered.

EUR.when: Sept 10, 12:15Z - TE model still carries 2.65% refi (2.50% depo) by quarter-end
EUR.note: Deposit facility re-verified on TE at 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike; main refinancing 2.40%, marginal lending 2.65%. Use the 2.25% depo. EUR holds +2 and is now the widest gap on the board, because it is the only currency whose inflation problem is domestic rather than borrowed from crude: July HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5% from 2.4% and services 3.4%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, August composite PMI 52.1 and a nine-month high with manufacturing 52.8 and a four-year high, unemployment stable at 6.3%. The gas leg has weakened - TTF is 64.36 EUR/MWh and -3.54%, off Monday's three-and-a-half-year high of 68.46, though EU storage at roughly 63% is the lowest for the date since 2009, which keeps a floor under it. Two events frame the euro from here. Today at 11:30Z the July meeting accounts: with the energy argument softer, a dovish set of accounts is the main threat to +2, and the June accounts language to compare against is that second-round effects were not yet observed but risks were rising with the duration of the shock. Tomorrow at 07:00Z Spain's flash August CPI, where consensus is 4.2% against 3.6% prior - a jump of that size drags the area flash on Tuesday and would hard-wire September 10. Counterweights unchanged: negotiated wages slowed to 2.44% from 2.56%, consumer inflation expectations fell a third month to 2.9%.

GBP.when: Sept 17, 11:00Z - Jul 30 was a 6-3 hold with three voting for 4.00%
GBP.note: Bank Rate re-verified on TE at 3.75%. GBP holds +1 and continues to trade on yield rather than policy: the 10-year gilt at 4.997% is still the highest in the G10, and cable is 1.36291 after touching 1.3670 on Aug 21, its best since mid-February, on stronger-than-forecast August flash PMIs. The underlying data is genuinely two-sided. Prices: July CPI 2.9% from 2.6% and a four-month high, but the driver was the 13% Ofgem cap uplift with energy inflation 9.8% from 5.7%, while core held FLAT at 2.6% for a third month and services COOLED to 3.4% from 3.6%. Labour: unemployment 4.9% against 4.8% expected, employment change +83k from +147k, average earnings including bonus 4.1% from 4.4%, HMRC payrolls -12.85k. Activity: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q from +0.6%, annual 1.2%. The MPC has said it stands ready to tighten further and markets still price a quarter point by November, but the energy channel that was going to rescue the three dissenters weakened with the gas complex this week. No UK data of consequence before September 17. Express sterling against the loonie, the dollar and now the kiwi and the franc - not against the euro or the Aussie.

JPY.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 1.00%, the highest since September 1995, held Jul 31 in an 8-1 vote with Takata dissenting for 1.25%. JPY holds +1. The domestic case keeps improving in exactly the place the Bank says it is watching: July services producer prices accelerated to +3.6% y/y against 3.2% expected, national CPI 1.9% and a seven-month high, core 1.8% from 1.6%, core-core 1.9%, ex-fresh-food-and-policy-effects 2.3%, cash earnings +3.4% with real earnings positive a sixth month, unemployment 2.5%, jobs-to-applications 1.18. The July Summary of Opinions flagged room to keep hiking with one view that hikes could come faster than markets expect, and the June minutes had most members seeing higher crude costs broadening into consumer prices. The tape is the problem: USD/JPY is 159.093 after the first joint US-Japan intervention since 2011 on Aug 1, which followed a 40-year high of 163.73 and drove the pair to 155-156 before it retraced. No follow-up action since. The external account still caps the score - import prices +29.1% y/y - although four sessions of falling crude begin to repair it. Near-term risk is tonight: Tokyo August CPI at 23:30Z with core consensus 1.7% against 1.9% prior, i.e. a SOFT consensus that could take the edge off September pricing. That is why USD/JPY steps back from HIGH to MEDIUM even though 160 remains the defined invalidation and the MoF sits on the same side as the trade.

AUD.when: Sept 29, 04:30Z - hike odds repriced to ~27% from ~17% after the July CPI beat
AUD.note: Cash rate re-verified on TE at 4.35%, the G10's highest, held Aug 11. AUD holds +1 with a second, independent confirmation arriving overnight. The monetary case is Tuesday's July CPI indicator: headline +1.0% m/m against 0.8% forecast with the annual rate at 3.5%, well above the 3.2-3.3% bank consensus, and critically the RBA's preferred trimmed mean +0.5% m/m against 0.3% leaving the annual trimmed mean UNCHANGED at 3.6%, its highest since September 2024. The breadth is the point - market goods and services ex volatile items +1.0% m/m and discretionary ex tobacco +1.5% - which is demand-side, not a petrol blip, and it validates the August minutes where the Board weighed a pre-emptive hike, said inflation is too high with excess demand persisting, did not discuss a cut, and cited Middle East oil and AI/data-centre capex as upside risks. Hauser on Aug 19: the RBA will need to raise again if upside risks materialise. The industrial confirmation is copper at a record 6.6956 USD/lb, +51.5% y/y. What keeps AUD at +1 rather than +2 is the labour market: July employment FELL 15,827 against +15-25k expected, part-time -32,160, unemployment 4.5% and a post-COVID high, wage growth 3.2%. AUD/USD 0.71851, +0.31%. Q2 capex today, Q2 GDP Sept 2 (TE forecast 0.0% q/q).

NZD.when: Sept 2, 02:00Z - DOWNGRADED to a coin flip; consensus is +25bp to 2.75% but market pricing is close to three-way
NZD.note: OCR re-verified on TE at 2.50% after the Jul 8 hike, the first in three years. NZD is CUT from +1 to 0 today, and the reason is that its hawkish case turns out to have been an oil trade. The 4.1% Q2 CPI that anchored the score - the highest since Q4 2023 and well above the 1-3% band - was led by transport +10.6% with petrol +27.5%, and the RBNZ's own July MPS said explicitly that the partial reopening of the Strait of Hormuz had lowered global oil, gas and petrochemical prices and eased near-term inflation pressure, projecting headline to fall from its Q2 peak toward 2% over twelve months and saying only that further increases remain POSSIBLE with the pace data-dependent. Crude has now fallen a fourth straight session on the Iran-Oman corridor framework. What is left underneath is weak: unemployment 5.6% and the highest since Q3 2015, underutilisation 13.8% from 12.9%, wage growth 2.1%, two-year inflation expectations down to 2.34%, TE's own Q3 GDP forecast at MINUS 0.1% q/q for the September 16 release, manufacturing PMI down to 54.3 from 60.1 and services at 50.6. Governor Breman's sooner-and-more-sharply line is from a May 29 speech and is not current guidance. NZD/USD 0.59567 and -0.34%, the worst major overnight. Trade the kiwi SHORT against the euro, the Aussie and the yen, keep it a low-conviction long against the dollar and the loonie only, and size September 2 as a real two-way event.

CAD.when: Sept 2, 13:45Z - a seventh straight hold (note: sources conflict between Sept 2 and Sept 3)
CAD.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 2.25%, held Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting; Bank Rate 2.5%, deposit 2.20%. CAD stays at MINUS 1. The oil engine has now failed for a fourth consecutive session - WTI 80.57 and Brent 86.49, with Brent down roughly 3% over three days - and the trade war is live: Champagne's 99-page list covers C$27.6bn (about US$19.9bn) of American goods at 15%, 25% and 50% across roughly 700 product lines from September 8, matching the new US 50% duties on about US$20bn of Canadian imports imposed after Carney suspended talks, alongside a C$7.5bn domestic support package and reports Washington is weighing further escalation. Domestic activity was already soft: composite PMI 49.7 and services 49.1 both contracting, retail sales -0.8% m/m, quarterly GDP 0.0% with annual -0.1%. The offsets are real but not enough - July CPI 3.0% at the ceiling of the control range with gasoline +25.7% y/y, employment +75.1k and unemployment at a two-year low of 6.4%, monthly GDP +0.2% in June. A bank near the lower end of neutral will not tighten into contracting services and a tariff shock. Be explicit about the risk though: Q2 GDP lands tomorrow at 12:30Z with consensus of +3.4% ANNUALISED against -0.1% prior, and TE's own forecast is +0.8% q/q. That is the single cleanest way for a CAD short to be hurt this week - a big beat would force a re-look at the score. USD/CAD 1.38623.

CHF.when: Sept 24, 07:30Z - Reuters poll unanimously expects zero, held through 2026
CHF.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 0.00%, held Mar 19 and Jun 18. CHF is CUT from +1 to 0 today because the leg that justified the score has stopped working. The franc has failed to lead a haven move three separate times now, and the cleanest evidence is the cross: EUR/CHF sits near 0.938, which is not haven behaviour against the strongest currency on the board, and the franc has notably NOT outperformed the euro through the entire war. With the Iran-Oman corridor framework negotiating the premium away and gold slipping 0.72% to 4,624.75, the bid is fading rather than building. What remains is a funding-currency profile: July CPI 0.4% from 0.5% and a four-month low with the first monthly fall in six, core 0.3% unchanged, producer and import prices deflating, unemployment risen to 3.0% NSA with 139,276 unemployed and vacancies down 2,088, wage growth 1.8%, and an SNB forecast of only 0.6% inflation for 2026 and 2027. And the central bank is on the other side: Schlegel has repeated his readiness to intervene against rapid or excessive appreciation, and FX reserves rose to CHF 768.3bn in July. The real economy is the counterargument and it is strong - Q2 GDP +1.5% q/q, the best since 2021, plus a record July trade surplus of CHF 8,141mn and a services PMI at 63.9 - but a good chunk of that is pharma front-running US tariffs and will not repeat. USD/CHF 0.80390, Swiss 10y 0.361%. Keep the franc long only against the dollar and the loonie; it is now SHORT against the euro, the yen, the Aussie and sterling.

catalysts.event: Iran-Oman Hormuz corridor talks (30-60 day window)
catalysts.note: The Aug 25 framework covers a temporary joint navigation corridor, joint mine-clearing and technical talks toward a permanent arrangement - but on Aug 26 the IRGC said the Strait stays CLOSED until the US honours the Islamabad MoU, and a senior official demanded an end to the war plus financial compensation. Qatar's PM was in Tehran on Aug 27. Any re-closure headline reverses the entire oil-down trade and with it CAD, NZD, CHF, XAU and USOIL.

The first joint US-Japan intervention since 2011 came on Aug 1 after USD/JPY hit a 40-year high of 163.73. The pair fell to 155-156 and has retraced to 159.09 with no follow-up action since. 160 is the line that matters.

geopolitics: The war that began with US-Israel strikes on Feb 28 is in a phase of negotiated, contested de-escalation, and the FX transmission is now running through more currencies than it was a week ago. On Aug 25 in Tehran, Iran's Araghchi and Oman's Al Busaidi announced a phased framework: a temporary joint navigation corridor through the Strait of Hormuz with the inbound leg entirely in Iranian waters and the outbound leg through Iranian and Omani waters, a joint mine-clearing project, and technical talks over the next 30 to 60 days toward a permanent corridor and its administration, with the two countries also reportedly settling shares of Hormuz waters and related revenues. Trump declared the same day that all mines in the Strait have been removed or detonated and warned that any vessel laying new ones will be destroyed. But the framework is not an opening. On Aug 26 the IRGC said that while Iran and Oman had agreed terms, the United States is the obstacle and the Strait remains CLOSED until Washington honours the Islamabad memorandum, and a senior official added that there will be no full reopening without an end to the war plus financial compensation. Araghchi has said Iran will not accept a ceasefire, only an end to the war. That sits against Bessent's Aug 23-24 'economic D-Day' sanctions package targeting aviation, shipping, technology, gold and digital assets, which drew Iranian threats of ship seizures, and Trump's Aug 17 refusal to extend the ceasefire along with a threat to bomb Oman if it interferes. Qatar's Prime Minister was in Tehran today discussing de-escalation and the restoration of pre-Feb-28 freedom of navigation. Markets have chosen to trade the framework rather than the caveat: WTI is 80.57 and Brent 86.49 on a fourth straight down session, roughly 3% lower over three days, EU TTF gas is 64.36 EUR/MWh and down 3.54% from Monday's three-and-a-half-year high of 68.46, and gold has slipped 0.72% to 4,624.75. The FX read is that the de-escalation has now moved past its first-order victim and is claiming its second and third. CAD was the obvious one and stays at -1. NZD is the new casualty, because its 4.1% Q2 CPI was a fuel print - transport +10.6%, petrol +27.5% - and the RBNZ explicitly cited the Hormuz reopening as the reason inflation returns to 2%. CHF is the mirror image: its bid was the war itself, and with EUR/CHF near 0.938 the franc has never actually outperformed the euro through this conflict. The beneficiaries are the currencies whose inflation is domestic - EUR on core at 2.5% and services at 3.4%, AUD on a trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% - plus JPY, whose +29.1% y/y import-price drag finally starts to heal. Two things temper it. EU gas storage is only about 63% full, the lowest for the date since 2009, so the European energy floor is high regardless. And the whole trade is one IRGC headline from reversing, which is why USOIL and XAU carry oversized risk notes today rather than oversized positions.
